author: ribeye
dek: A Canton couple's parents-weekend flight to Boston was cancelled as a slow-moving nor'easter flooded coastal streets, cut power to about 100,000 customers, and killed one worker in Brooklyn.
disclaimer: Parody: the Becker family of Canton is fictional. The September nor'easter is real, as reported by the Associated Press in September 2026.
headline: Canton Family's Boston Trip Washes Out as Nor'easter Floods the Northeast

ohio_story: CANTON, Ohio — Tom and Rita Becker of Canton had done everything right. They booked their flights out of Akron-Canton Airport weeks ago, packed a cooler of buckeyes for their daughter's dorm at Boston University, and even ironed the matching McKinley Bulldogs sweatshirts they planned to wear to parents weekend. Then the nor'easter parked itself off the East Coast on Saturday, and their flight to Boston Logan was cancelled along with hundreds of others, leaving the Beckers watching the Weather Channel from their couch on Fulton Road while the rain they were supposed to be dodging fell on somebody else's coastline instead.

"We were going to Boston. We ended up in Belden Village," Tom said, gesturing at the shopping bags by the door. "Rita said if we couldn't see our daughter, we could at least buy her a new lamp, which is the most Canton solution to a hurricane-adjacent problem I have ever heard." Their daughter, meanwhile, sent them a video of her dormmates kayaking down a flooded street in Boston — a video Tom has now watched eleven times — and a photo of a tree down across the quad, which Rita has printed out and stuck to the fridge next to the Pro Football Hall of Fame magnet. "She says she's fine, the dining hall has power, and the game is still on," Rita said. "I told her to stay inside, and she told me she's from Stark County, Mom, we invented staying inside."

The Beckers have rescheduled for next month, assuming the Atlantic cooperates, and Tom has already started a spreadsheet ranking alternate weekends, alternate airports, and — in a column Rita describes as "completely unnecessary" — alternate daughters' colleges in states without oceans. For now, the cooler of buckeyes is in the freezer, the sweatshirts are folded and waiting, and the lamp is boxed up by the front door, ready for the next attempt. "Boston can keep its twenty-foot waves," Tom said. "We've got Lake Cable, we've got Gervasi, and we've got a daughter who thinks a nor'easter is just a snow day with better branding."
real_summary: A slow-moving, powerful nor'easter crept along the coast of the U.S. Northeast on Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026, producing high winds that caused power outages while whipping up big waves and heavy rains. The New York City Housing Authority said one of its employees was killed by a fallen tree in Brooklyn as the storm pelted the city with rain and strong winds. Emergency crews in mid-Atlantic and New England states raced to restore power after downed trees contributed to outages for about 100,000 customers in the region.

Tens of millions of people remained in the path of the storm for Sunday, with major flooding forecast for some coastal areas. The Federal Emergency Management Agency said response coordination centers in impacted regions were operating at an "enhanced posture," and teams were on standby in New England in case of widespread outages. Bob Oravec, lead forecaster with the National Weather Service in College Park, Maryland, said there would be "a lot of high winds, a lot of high tides and heavy rain possibility over the next few days for the northeastern U.S." The highest tides were likely north of Atlantic City, New Jersey, from Saturday night into Sunday, creating the potential for widespread road flooding in coastal and bayside communities.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul warned that coastal flooding was the biggest threat, but said heavy rains, powerful winds and waves as high as 20 feet were also expected, telling residents, "Anyone who goes in or near the water this weekend is literally gambling with their life." In New Jersey and New York, some people kayaked down flooded streets. Hundreds of flights were canceled at Boston Logan International Airport, as were the vast majority of flights at Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket, and a flooding-related highway closure on North Carolina's Hatteras Island scrambled a wedding, stranding most of the couple's roughly 45 guests on the mainland.
source_note: AP reporting, Sep. 26-27, 2026: nor'easter flooding, outages and one death in the Northeast; Boston Logan cancellations and Hatteras Island wedding disruption.
